title: Efo Elegusi
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: The egusi that is never fried and never balled — blended smooth with onion and crayfish and stirred into a fried pepper base, deliberately on the watery side.
longDesc: Of the four egusi techniques this is the one that takes a position. The ground seed is mixed smooth with blended onion and two tablespoons of crayfish and stirred straight into the stew, where it dissolves — no pre-frying in oil, no balls dropped into stock. The author says why: she is not a fan of clumpy egusi and prefers hers a little watery, like egusi ijebu. The useful conversion on the page is that one and a half cups of whole seed gives one cup ground, which no other source states.
ingredients: Assorted meats — beef, ponmo, goat meat, cow leg, shaki and other offals are ideal
1 1/2 cups whole egusi, or 1 cup ground egusi
1/2 cup raw or cooked king prawns (optional)
steps: Blend the bell peppers, scotch bonnet and one onion roughly. Grind the egusi if you bought it whole.
Heat the palm oil on medium and add half the chopped onion.
Saute until fragrant, then add the blended pepper mix and the bouillon cube. Do not add salt if you are using seasoned meat stock.
Fry the pepper mix 10 minutes, until reduced by almost half and the palm oil settles on top.
Add 1 to 2 cups of stock and cook 5 minutes.
Meanwhile blend the remaining half onion smooth, add it to the egusi with 2 tablespoons of the crayfish, and mix until smooth.
Add the egusi paste to the stew, stir, and cook 5 minutes.
Add the meats, smoked or stockfish, prawns and the remaining tablespoon of crayfish. Season.
Add the ugwu leaves and cook 2 minutes.
Add the efinrin or basil and cook 2 minutes.
Take it off the heat and let it simmer 2 to 3 minutes on the residual heat.
chefTips: One and a half cups of whole egusi grinds down to one cup. That conversion is on the page and it is the only one in any source consulted.
The egusi is mixed with blended onion and crayfish before it goes anywhere near the pot. That is what lets it dissolve instead of clumping.
No salt if your stock is seasoned. Between the stock, the cube and three heaped tablespoons of crayfish there is plenty.
The pepper base wants ten minutes and the cue is the oil settling on top — the same signal as every other Nigerian fried pepper base.
Efinrin goes in after the ugwu, two minutes each, and the pot comes off the heat. Basil is a finishing herb here, not a cooking one.
Watery is intentional. If you want it thick you are making a different dish — see NGA011 or NGA014.
Ugwu is the author's preference alongside efinrin. Both are added chopped and raw.
commonMistakes: Frying the egusi in oil first.
Adding the ground seed dry to the pot.
Salting on top of a seasoned stock.
Cooking the basil for more than two minutes.
Thickening it until it is no longer egusi ijebu.
sources: Adapted from 'Egusi Soup – Efo Elegusi', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: 1.5 cups whole egusi or 1 cup ground, 1/2 cup palm oil, 1-2 cups chicken or meat stock, 3 red bell peppers, 2 medium onions, 2 scotch bonnet, 1 cup chopped ugu leaves, 1/2 cup efinrin or basil, 3 heaped tablespoons ground crayfish, 1/4 cup smoked prawns (optional), 1 medium smoked fish or stockfish, 1/2 cup raw or cooked king prawns (optional), 1 bouillon cube, salt to taste. The 10-minute pepper fry, the 5 minutes with stock, the 5 minutes after the egusi goes in, the 5 to 7 minutes with the proteins, the 2 minutes each for ugwu and basil and the 2-to-3-minute residual finish are all hers.

Her stated preference, quoted: 'I'm not a fan of clumpy Egusi soup, I prefer mine a tad bit watery, very much like Egusi Ijebu.' This is the clearest statement of partisanship in the corpus consulted — she names the style she rejects and the regional style she aligns with.
NOTE: the assorted meats carry no quantity on the page.

ETHNOGRAPHIC DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled. Kitchen Butterfly's Edo egusi page calls the watery, evenly dispersed style the IGBO version, contrasting it with the Edo and Yoruba ball technique. Sisi Jemimah, a Yoruba author who prefers watery, calls it 'very much like Egusi Ijebu' — that is, Yoruba. Two sources assign the same technique to different peoples. Both are recorded.

GAP: 1Q Food Platter's 'How to Cook Egusi Ijebu' was located but not retrieved. Since Sisi Jemimah defines her preferred style by reference to egusi ijebu, that page would be the obvious next source for this entry.
Egusi has four documented techniques: frying (NGA012), caking (NGA011), balling (NGA014) and dissolving (this one).
reheating: Low heat with a splash of stock. It thickens as it stands, so expect to loosen it.
healthBenefits: Melon seed supplies protein, magnesium and zinc.
Scent leaf and basil carry aromatic oils with antimicrobial activity.
Red palm oil provides carotenoids and vitamin E.
culturalNote: Ijebu cooking has its own reputation within Yorubaland — the Ijebu are credited with ikokore, with a particular way of making egusi, and with a general willingness to do things differently from Ibadan or Lagos. Egusi ijebu is thin where other egusi is thick, and a cook who makes it that way is usually making a point rather than an error.
